prime.problem: The five cards each fix one way an agent eval lies: the wrong grader, the wrong count, the wrong error bar, too few tasks, or no gate. Read one at a time, it's easy to fix the bar and miss that the verdicts underneath it were wrong.
prime.fits: The map for course 4. It builds on the claim chain from course 1 (a 'done' needs evidence per link) and on measuring an agent from the hub, and puts the five cards in the order a number has to pass through them.
prime.goal: Take any eval number and say which of the five checks it has passed, which one it fails first, and which card fixes it.

attend: Why does the decision table put the grader first, ahead of the statistics?
In the mental model, why is power analysis drawn as a bracket rather than a box on the pipeline?
Which lever rows are exact arithmetic, and which come from simulations or illustrative numbers?
Where does the judge that reads the summary sit, and why is it red rather than grey?
When does the overview say pass@k, not pass^k, is the honest number?

must: Every later check computes on the grader's verdicts → a grader that reads the agent's summary passes the Tuesday run's false claim → pass^k, a clustered bar and 136 tasks then measure the wrong thing precisely → fix the grader first
Users meet the agent on every run, and failures cluster on hard tasks → report pass^k counted per task (C(c,k) ÷ C(n,k)), averaged over tasks → pass@k and the plug-in both flatter reliability
Trials of one task share its difficulty → the task is the unit for error bars and for sample size → cluster and pair by task, and add tasks, not repeats, when the bar is too wide

A number changes nothing until someone acts on it → an owner, a regression case and a per-slice gate with hard blockers → otherwise the same failure ships again after the next model, prompt or grader change
reference: the per-row effect sizes in the ranked table
which post covers which card (Part 8, Data Part 7, Wolfe's two posts, Miller)
the glossary cells: output vs outcome, avg@k, MDE

compress.prompt: Card closed: write the five checks in order, each as a question with its card. Then draw the mental model: the pipeline from run to what ships, the red judge branch, the grey dashboard, the power-analysis bracket and the loop back through an owner.
checklist: 1 is the verdict true (outcome, deterministic first) → graders
2 does it count what users get (pass^k per task) → pass-k
3 is the bar honest (cluster, pair by task) → error bars
4 could you have seen it (task count before running) → power analysis
5 does it change what ships (owner, regression case, per-slice gate) → evidence loop
a later check can't repair an earlier one

retrieve.q: Explain why a tight, well-powered error bar can still describe a false number, using the Tuesday run.
answer: the bar measures sampling noise in the verdicts, not whether the verdicts are true
a judge reading the compaction summary passes the run the checker fails
so every trial like it counts as a pass, and more tasks only tighten the bar around the wrong rate

retrieve.q: Walk a proposed claim, 'compaction raises false success claims', through the five checks for a 30 tasks × 3 repeats design. Which check fails first?
answer: 1: grade with the checker's re-run, not the message: passes if built that way
2: report the false-claim rate and pass^k per task
4 fails: 30 × 3 sees only Δ ≥ 0.222 at ρ 0.2; a 10-point rise needs 136 tasks

retrieve.q: You have one week. Your team has a dashboard of average pass rate from an LLM judge on 20 tasks, run once each. Which single fix do you make first, and what do you give up?
answer: the grader first: code on the outcome, so the verdicts are true
then a gate on known regressions, because it stops repeats even with small n
you give up being able to call small gains real: 20 tasks run once can only see large effects

compare.q: The hub's coding-agent overview ranked levers by tokens, cost and trust in the result, around one formula. This overview has no formula, only an ordered table. What about the evidence problem makes an ordering the right shape, and which lever appears in both?
answer: token cost adds up across terms, so levers trade off on one formula
evidence fails in sequence: a later check can't repair an earlier one, so order is the relationship
repeats with an honest interval, and hidden tests or an outside checker, appear in both

compare.q: The claim chain splits one run's 'done' into five links; this overview splits one eval number into five checks. Where do the two meet, and what does each catch that the other doesn't?
answer: they meet at the grader: an outcome grader checks link 4, effect verified
the claim chain judges one run; the five checks judge a number over many runs and whether it changes what ships
the chain can't tell noise from a real change; the checks don't say which link inside a run broke

predict.q: Suppose the grader's mistakes line up with the agent's: the judge passes every false claim. Before revealing, which of checks 2 to 5 would notice anything wrong?
predict.answer: None of them. pass^k would read higher than the truth, the clustered and paired bars would be tight around the wrong rate, a power analysis would happily size the experiment, and the gate would ship. The statistics only see disagreement between trials, not between the verdict and the world. That is why the overview ranks the grader first and why the open-questions card's top item asks what a judge sees.

apply.task: Pick one eval number your team uses (or the capstone's planned 30 tasks × 3 repeats measuring false claims). Write one line per check: what it does today, pass or fail, and the cheapest fix from the matching card. Mark the first check that fails.
apply.done: You have five lines, the first failing check is marked, and its fix names a card. For the capstone design that is check 4: 30 × 3 has 27.4% power for a 10-point rise at ρ 0.2, and 136 tasks give 80%.
apply.hint: Start at check 1 and stop at the first failure; anything after it is premature.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how many later checks catch a biased grader?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the checks have an order, or why the gate comes last?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: shared task difficulty → clustered bars, or clustered bars → task counts?
Which of the five checks does your own eval fail first?
Which card do you need to reread before the training course turns graders into rewards?
